interfaces: AssignmentLockStore.release(request): LockResult, request accepts optional expectedOwnerId/expectedRunId/expectedCanonicalBranch compare-and-swap guards (BOOT-025) checked atomically against the same read that decides whether to mutate anything

behavioralConstraints: release() claims the active record via an atomic rename before inspecting or mutating it, then checks lockId plus any supplied expectedOwnerId/expectedRunId/expectedCanonicalBranch guards against that exact claimed content — never a separate, earlier read a concurrent recoverStale() could invalidate before the actual mutation runs; a mismatch on any one rejects the entire call as LOCK_ID_MISMATCH with no partial effect and restores the claimed record to the active path byte-for-byte (or, if a third operation has since created its own fresh record there, leaves that record untouched instead of overwriting it), and omitting all three optional guards preserves the original lockId-only match exactly

release() writes an exclusive reservation marker before ever claiming the active path away, and holds it for the call's entire duration (removed only in a finally once the call resolves): acquire() checks for this marker the same way it already checks for an in-flight recoverStale() claim (after its own exclusive-create write succeeds, rolling that write back if a marker is found), so ordinary acquisition stays blocked for release()'s full window rather than observing the active path as transiently free while release() is still deciding what to do with the content it claimed

if the content release() claims away is unreadable or fails to parse as JSON, the claim is restored to the active path (renamed back) before the read failure is rethrown, rather than the claimed record silently vanishing along with the claim file — a caller that catches and normalizes the throw still finds an active assignment to retry against, not a task that falsely appears to have none

a rename failure while release() claims the active path is reported as LOCK_NOT_FOUND only when the underlying error is ENOENT (a genuinely absent lock); any other rename failure (a permission error, a read-only filesystem, a transient I/O error) propagates rather than being reported the same way, since a caller that treats LOCK_NOT_FOUND as benign would otherwise skip release entirely while the original assignment remains present on disk

requireDate (acquiredAt/expiresAt/occurredAt) accepts a seconds value of 60 only at the UTC-equivalent instant 23:59:60 — computed from the timestamp's own offset, not requiring the literal local digits to read 23:59 — consistent with control-plane.controlled-merge's and control-plane.evidence-store's own leap-second validators

isStale's expiresAt-vs-now comparison and validateAcquire's expiresAt-later-than-acquiredAt check both go through the same leap-second-substituted instant requireDate's own Date.parse sanity check uses, rather than a raw Date.parse on the original string: Date.parse of an unsubstituted leap second is NaN, which would otherwise make an expiry ordering check unable to reject a bad order and make a lock with a leap-second expiresAt appear never-expiring, permanently blocking explicit stale recovery. A leap second (with any fractional part it may carry) always maps to exactly 1ms before the following minute's own instant, computed from the whole-second ':59' form with any fraction discarded — not a flat +1000ms added on top of the substituted parse, which both collides exactly with the next minute for a fraction-less leap second and, for a leap second carrying its own fraction (':60.500', say), can add on top of that flat offset and land the result *past* the next minute entirely, comparing a late-fraction leap second as later than a minute that is chronologically after it. This system has no need to distinguish between two different leap-second instants down to the millisecond, only to place any leap second strictly between the ':59' second before it and the next minute

release()'s reservation marker and the record it claims away both use a fixed, well-known path (not a randomized one) once the reservation is held, since the reservation itself already guarantees only one release() is ever in flight for a task at a time; if the marker is found older than a fixed staleness threshold (mirroring control-plane.controlled-merge's own STALE_LOCK_MS convention for an abandoned holder) by acquire() or a later release() call, that reclaim is itself atomic — not a plain stat-then-unlink: the marker is claimed via its own atomic rename first, and only the *captured* file's own re-checked age (rename preserves mtime) decides whether to proceed, restoring it untouched if it turns out to be a fresh marker a different, legitimately live release() call created in the gap between the initial staleness check and this claim — a bare stat-then-unlink could otherwise strip that live call of its own protection mid-flight. Once a claimed marker is confirmed genuinely stale, the orphaned claimed record — if the crash happened after the active path was renamed away but before it was restored or finished — is restored to the active path via an exclusive-create write (never a plain renameSync, which POSIX silently allows to overwrite an existing destination file rather than fail — a concurrent, legitimate acquire() that already created a fresh record at the active path during this exact reclaim window, which acquire()'s own recognition of the marker's temporary '.reclaim' claim keeps as narrow as an ordinary single ownership check, must never be clobbered by the orphan) before the stale marker itself is dropped; ordinary acquisition is never granted merely because the marker looks fresh-vacant without this check running first, since #hasReleaseClaim also recognizes that temporary '.reclaim' claim as blocking
